bib.title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting

question: Can randomly dropping units during training prevent overfitting and approximate averaging an exponential number of networks cheaply?
hypothesis: Dropout prevents co-adaptation of hidden units, and a single net with weights scaled by p at test time approximates the average of the thinned nets.
contributions: Dropout: randomly drop units during training, scale weights by p at test time
Evidence of gains across vision, speech, text and computational biology
Analysis of marginalised dropout (linear regression equals a form of ridge regression)

method.summary: Each training case uses a thinned network sampled by Bernoulli(p) masks on units; trained with SGD, max-norm, high momentum. Test uses the unthinned net with outgoing weights multiplied by p. Evaluated on MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, TIMIT, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.split: 10,000 train images held out for validation, then merged for final training

datasets.name: SVHN
datasets.split: 6000 validation (400/class standard + 200/class extra); not merged back
datasets.preprocessing: RGB normalised to zero mean unit variance

datasets.name: CIFAR-10/100
datasets.preprocessing: global contrast normalisation per channel then ZCA whitening

datasets.name: TIMIT
datasets.preprocessing: Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment, 21-frame windows, mean/variance normalised

models.name: Dropout feed-forward nets (MNIST)
models.init_from: random, or RBM/DBN/DBM pretraining (weights scaled by 1/p)

models.name: Dropout convnet (SVHN, CIFAR)
models.architecture: 3 conv (96, 128 and 256 filters, 5x5, stride 1) each + 3x3 max-pool stride 2, then 2 FC of 2048, ReLU

models.name: ImageNet convnet
models.architecture: Krizhevsky et al. 2012; details not given here

training.objective: supervised classification loss under random unit dropout; RBM variant uses CD-1
training.lr: 10-100x the no-dropout optimum (guide); TIMIT 0.1, 0.01 for DBN finetuning
training.dropout: p=0.5 hidden, 0.8 input (MNIST); SVHN/CIFAR p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); TIMIT 0.8 input / 0.5 hidden; splicing 0.5 hidden / 0.7 input
training.regularisation: max-norm ||w||2<=c: c=2 MNIST, c=4 SVHN/TIMIT, typical 3-4
training.seeds: 10 seeds for Table 10; otherwise not stated

inference.samples: weight scaling by p at test time; Monte-Carlo k sampled nets compared up to k~120

metrics.name: top-5 error
metrics.definition: correct label not among 5 most probable

metrics.name: Code Quality
metrics.definition: sum of p log(q/pbar) over examples, tissues, states (negative KL, higher better)

eval.protocol: Hyperparameters tuned on validation set; single reported runs for most tables (seeds not stated)

results.claim: Dropout lowers permutation-invariant MNIST error from 1.60% (standard net) to 1.35% with logistic units.
results.setup: MNIST, 3x1024 logistic net, p=0.5 hidden, 0.8 input
results.quote: With dropout the error reduces to 1.35%.

results.claim: Dropout with ReLU and max-norm gets 1.06% on MNIST (3x1024).
results.quote: Adding max-norm regularization again reduces it to 1.06%.

results.claim: A 2x8192 dropout net with over 65M parameters trained on 60,000 images reaches 0.95% without early stopping.
results.quote: A neural net with 2 layers and 8192 units per layer gets down to 0.95% error.

results.claim: DBM-pretrained dropout-finetuned net reaches 0.79% on permutation-invariant MNIST.
results.quote: DBM—pretrained dropout nets achieve a test error of 0.79%

results.claim: Dropout on SVHN convnet: 3.95% -> 3.02% (dropout in FC layers) -> 2.55% (dropout in all layers).
results.quote: Adding dropout to the convolutional layers as well further reduces the error to 2.55%.

results.claim: CIFAR-10 error drops from 15.60 (hand-tuned convnet) to 12.61 with dropout in every layer; CIFAR-100 from 43.48 to 37.20.
results.setup: CIFAR-10, no data augmentation, convnet as SVHN
results.quote: and adding dropout in every layer further reduces the error to 12.61%.

results.claim: Dropout convnet won ILSVRC-2012 with about 16% top-5 test error versus about 26% for standard vision features.
results.setup: ILSVRC-2012, average of 5 convnets + dropout (Krizhevsky et al. 2012)
results.table: Table 6, row Avg of 5 Conv Nets + dropout, column Top-5 (test)

results.claim: ILSVRC-2010 convnet with dropout: 37.5 top-1 / 17.0 top-5, versus 45.7 / 25.7 for SIFT+Fisher vectors.
results.table: Table 5, row Conv Net + dropout, column Top-1

results.claim: TIMIT phone error rate: 6-layer net 23.4% -> 21.8% with dropout; pretrained nets 22.7% -> 19.7%.
results.setup: TIMIT core test set, 21 log-filterbank frames, p=0.8 input 0.5 hidden, max-norm c=4
results.quote: A 6-layer net gives a phone error rate of 23.4%. Dropout further improves it to 21.8%.

results.claim: Reuters-RCV1 gain is small: 31.05% -> 29.62%.
results.setup: Reuters RCV1 subset, 402,738 docs, 2000-word bag of words, 50 classes
results.quote: Adding dropout reduced the error to 29.62%.

results.claim: On small alternative splicing data, dropout net scores 567 bits Code Quality, beating non-Bayesian baselines but below the Bayesian NN at 623.
results.setup: Alternative Splicing, 2932 train/733 test, 2x1024 dropout net, 5 folds
results.table: Table 8, row Neural Network with dropout, column Code Quality (bits)

results.claim: On MNIST 784-1024-1024-2048-10 ReLU, dropout+max-norm gives 1.05% versus 1.62% for L2 alone.
results.note: Table 2 prints 1.06 for a similar dropout+max-norm net
results.table: Table 9, row Dropout + Max-norm, column Test Classification error %

results.claim: Hidden-unit activation mean falls from about 2.0 to about 0.7 with dropout (sparser representations) in a 256-unit ReLU autoencoder.
results.setup: MNIST autoencoder, one hidden layer 256 ReLU, p=0.5
results.quote: The overall mean activation of hidden units is close to 2.0 for the autoencoder without dropout but drops to around 0.7 when dropout is used.

results.claim: Test error is flat for 0.4 <= p <= 0.8 with fixed n; default p=0.5 is near optimal.
With pn fixed, error at p=0.1 falls from 2.7% to 1.7%.
results.setup: MNIST, pn=256 first two layers, 512 last
results.quote: for p = 0.1 it fell from 2.7% to 1.7%

results.claim: Dropout gives no gain at 100 or 500 training examples; benefit rises then declines with data size.
results.quote: for extremely small data sets (100, 500) dropout does not give any improvements.

results.claim: Monte-Carlo averaging matches weight scaling at about k=50 samples.
results.quote: It can be seen that around k = 50, the Monte-Carlo method becomes as good as the approximate method.

results.claim: Dropout training takes 2-3 times longer than standard training of the same architecture.
results.quote: A dropout network typically takes 2-3 times longer to train than a standard neural network of the same ar-

results.claim: Marginalised dropout in linear regression equals ridge regression with Gamma=(diag(X^T X))^(1/2) in expectation.
results.quote: dropout with linear regression is equivalent, in expectation, to ridge regression with a particular form for Γ.

results.claim: Gaussian multiplicative noise (sigma=sqrt((1-p)/p)) is slightly better: MNIST 0.95 vs 1.08 Bernoulli.
results.note: CIFAR-10 12.5 vs 12.6; authors call it preliminary
results.table: Table 10, row MNIST, column Gaussian dropout

results.claim: Heuristics: use at least n/p hidden units, 10-100x learning rate, momentum 0.95-0.99, max-norm c of 3 to 4.
results.quote: a good dropout net should have at least n/p units.

limits: Dropout increases training time 2-3x because gradient updates are noisy.
Bayesian neural nets beat dropout on the small splicing data (623 vs 567 bits).
Gain is small on large datasets such as Reuters, and nil at 100-500 MNIST examples.
Marginalised-dropout equivalence is derived only for linear regression; no closed form for deep nets.
Batch size, seeds and compute are mostly not stated; MNIST-scale MLPs and convnets only, no transformers or attention.
Gaussian dropout comparison is described as preliminary.
practices: Use p=0.5 for hidden units and about 0.8 for real-valued inputs (A.4)
Make the layer at least n/p units (A.1)
Raise learning rate 10-100x and momentum to 0.95-0.99 (A.2)
Pair dropout with max-norm c of 3-4 (A.3)
Scale pretrained weights by 1/p before dropout finetuning and use smaller learning rates (5.2)
Inverted dropout: multiply retained activations by 1/p in training, leave test weights unchanged (10)

code.snippet: r(l)_j ~ Bernoulli(p); y~(l) = r(l) * y(l); z(l+1)_i = w(l+1)_i y~(l) + b(l+1)_i; y(l+1)_i = f(z(l+1)_i). Test: W_test = p W
minimize_w ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Gamma w||^2, Gamma = (diag(X^T X))^(1/2)
